title: Troubleshooting R
text:
Encountering errors and unexpected results is an inevitable part of learning any programming language. The teaching staff is here to help, but before you send an email to your TA, its good to do a little troubleshooting to make sure the problem isn’t something you can solve on your own.
Every problem is different, but there are some steps that I generally recommend taking when you encounter a problem in R.

title: Troubleshooting R
text:
Step 0: Take a little break
In my experience, 99% of errors are the result of stuff like misspelling a variable or forgetting to load a package and they’re completely obvious once you’ve spotted them. There’s no way around this, it happens to everyone. The only real advice I can offer here is: take a break and relax your brain. Go for a walk. Eat a sandwich. Pet a cat, etc. Then come back with a fresh set of eyes and retrace your steps to see if you can spot something that looks out of place.
Once you’ve done this, take a look at the offending output and see if you can get any clues about its origins. When you see messages like: Error in foo() : could not find function "foo" or Error: object 'x' not found its often either a misspelling or its the result of a variable or function that hasn’t been loaded into R yet.
Other messages are a little harder to parse, but you can often copy-paste the error into a search engine and you’ll find that other people have gotten help for the same issue. R has a big community of users, and so there’s a good chance that someone else has encountered the same problem you’re having and has written about how to solve it. Similarly, if you’re having an issue with a particular function, consult the help file and see if you can find any useful information there.
When this fails, then move on to step 1.

title: Troubleshooting R
section: Step 1: Clear the environment and restart R
text:
Step 1: Clear the environment and restart R
Some errors are caused by unexpected interactions between different libraries or objects in the working environment. In order to rule out issues like this, you want to start with a “fresh” environment with no packages or data loaded.
To restart R, you can press Ctrl + Shift + F10, or just close and reopen R-Studio. Then, to clear the environment, just press the little broom 🧹 icon in the environment pane, or enter the following command into the console:

rm(list = ls())

title: Troubleshooting R
section: Step 2: Try to replicate the issue
text:
Step 2: Try to replicate the issue
Now that you have a fresh R instance, try to replicate your problem. Make a new script and call it something like “error_replication” and then try to replicate your error message in as few steps as possible. Remember that you’ll need to re-load any packages or data you’ve been using for your analysis first. For GVPT 201, that usually means at least running library(RCPA3) and possibly loading one of the world, nes, gss or states data sets.
Run through each line of code one step at a time until you encounter the problem. If you want to be absolutely sure that your code can be replicated, repeat step 1 and then press the “source” button at the top right of the script editor. This will run the entire script in sequence.
Here’s an example of a common error that comes from trying to use the max function on a variable that isn’t numeric. I might have a lot of other code in my original script, but I only need four lines to replicate this error message and you can easily recreate it yourself by copying these same lines:

# Step 1: After restarting Rstudio and clearing the environment...
# Step 2: I load the required packages ----
library(RCPA3)
# and import the "world" data set and assign it to a variable
world<-RCPA3::world

# Step 3: And then I recreate my error message----
max(world$election.violence.post)

Error in Summary.factor(structure(c(1L, NA, 1L, NA, 1L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, : 'max' not meaningful for factors


Isolating the problem like this can usually make it a lot easier to spot the source of the issue, but if you can replicate the error and you’re still not sure how to fix it, then its probably time to move on to the next step.

title: Troubleshooting R
text:
Step 3: Send an Email
If you’ve tried the previous steps and you still haven’t resolved your issue, its time to reach out to a classmate, TA, or the instructor. In order to make that process go as smoothly as possible, you want to be sure to pass along sufficient details about your issue so that someone else can help you troubleshoot. So generally this means including:

A description of the problem and what you’re trying to do
The text of the error message (if applicable) or a screenshot of the problematic output
A script that can replicate your problem in as few steps as possible (see step 2)

Here’s an example of how that email might look:







To: MySectionTA@umd.edu


From: me@umd.edu


Subject: GVPT 201: Error when using max


Hello, I’m working on the homework and I keep getting an error message when I try to use the max function.
The error message is: Error in Summary.factor(c(1L, NA, 1L, NA, 1L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, NA,:‘max’ not meaningful for factors
I’ve attached an Rscript that replicates the error below
Thank you!
[here, you would want to attach the error replication script from step 2]

text:
This page offers some additional code and examples for downloading and manipulating the survey data.
As always, you’ll want to load the RCPA3 package at the start of your analysis so you can use the additional functions you’re already familiar with.
library(RCPA3)

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Applying a new variable label
The gvpt_survey data set includes the exact wording of each question as a variable label. You’ll see labels appear automatically when you use functions like freqC, but you can also view them by using Hmisc::label(variable_name)1

Hmisc::label(gvpt_survey$electoral_college)

[1] "Thinking for a moment about the way in which the president is elected in this country, which would you prefer:"


If you have created a new variable, or if you want to replace an existing label with something shorter, you can just use Hmisc::label(varname) <- "New label". For example, the label for electoral_college is kind of long, and might not fit on a plot, so I could assign a shorter label to it like this:

Hmisc::label(gvpt_survey$electoral_college) <- "Support for electing president by popular vote"

And now we can view the label again to check that our code worked:

Hmisc::label(gvpt_survey$electoral_college)

[1] "Support for electing president by popular vote"

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Dropping levels
Many of the survey questions allow responses that are mostly ordinal except for a “Not sure” response that shows up as a final response option. Leaving this “Not sure” option in place breaks the ordering of our otherwise ordinal question, so we’ll often treat these answers as NA values (or combine them with another category)
For instance, left_right_scale asks respondents to rank their own political views on a scale from Far left to Far right, but a small number of respondents said they were Not sure where they fit on this scale. We’ll generally want to drop or reassign these responses so we can treat Q37 as an ordered variable.

levels(gvpt_survey$left_right_scale)

[1] "Far left"     "Left"         "Center-left"  "Center"       "Center-right"
[6] "Right"        "Far right"    "Not sure"    


One way we can get rid of these “Not sure” responses is by creating a new factor variable that doesn’t include “Not sure” as a valid level. This will cause those responses to automatically become NA values, which we can then easily ignore when we run a calculation on Q37.
In plain English, the code below is saying:
“Make a new column in the gvpt_survey dataframe called ‘lr_position’. The new variable will be an ordered factor variable with all the same levels from left_right_scale except for ‘Not sure’”

# The same levels in the SAME ORDER they appear when I run levels(gvpt_survey$left_right_scale) 
newlevels <- c("Far left", "Left", "Center-left", "Center", "Center-right", "Right","Far right")



gvpt_survey$lr_position <- factor(x = gvpt_survey$left_right_scale,
                                  ordered = TRUE,
                                  levels = newlevels)

Note here that “Not sure” is not a level for the new variable I just created:

levels(gvpt_survey$lr_position)

[1] "Far left"     "Left"         "Center-left"  "Center"       "Center-right"
[6] "Right"        "Far right"   


This kind of recoding is easy to mess up, so its always a good idea to check your results after you finish. You can use View(gvpt_survey) to bring up the data viewer and browse your results, or you can use freqC to get a frequency table, or just use the basic table function and check to make sure your results match your expectations.

table(gvpt_survey$left_right_scale)  # 36 not sure responses


    Far left         Left  Center-left       Center Center-right        Right 
         163          376          201           85           90           39 
   Far right     Not sure 
          17           36 

table(gvpt_survey$lr_position)  # the not sure responses are absent here, but everything else is identical


    Far left         Left  Center-left       Center Center-right        Right 
         163          376          201           85           90           39 
   Far right 
          17

Making a numeric variable
We’ll sometimes treat ordinal variables with 5 or more categories as if they were continuous. Doing this in R will typically require you to reclassify a factor variable as a number. Fortunately, this just requires us to use the as.numeric function:

gvpt_survey$lr_position_numeric<-as.numeric(gvpt_survey$lr_position)


freqC(gvpt_survey$lr_position_numeric, plot=FALSE)

Before you do this, you’ll want to make absolutely sure that the variable you’re using is truly ordinal, so be especially careful to check that you’ve properly handled “don’t know” or “unsure” responses that break the ordering of a question (see the previous section for how to do this). Treating “Don’t know” as an ordered response can lead to very misleading results.

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Combining levels
In some cases we may want to simplify our analyses by combining certain categories of a response. For instance, only 18 respondents said that social media had an “Extremely positive” effect on politics. This might not be enough people for a meaningful inference, so we could decide to collapse this five category response into three categories: negative, neutral, and positive.



Do you believe that social media has a positive or negative influence on American politics?
 
  
    sm_effects 
    n 
    percent 
    cumulative percent 
  
 

  
    Extremely negative 
    228 
    23.5% 
    23.5% 
  
  
    Somewhat negative 
    440 
    45.4% 
    68.9% 
  
  
    Neither positive nor negative 
    145 
    14.9% 
    83.8% 
  
  
    Somewhat positive 
    139 
    14.3% 
    98.1% 
  
  
    Extremely positive 
    18 
    1.9% 
    100.0% 
  





Conceptually, I want to do a transformation that remaps the values like this:

Extremely negative → negative
Somewhat negative → negative
Neither positive nor negative → neutral
Somewhat positive → positive
Extremely positive → positive

There are actually several ways to do this. You can see some alternative approaches by clicking the tabs below:

Using logical statementsUsing factor() with labels =Using the forcats package


We can use boolean operators to selectively assign values to a vector and then declare that vector as a factor variable. To make this work, I’ll start with an empty factor called sm_effects_3cat.

# creating an empty factor variable with all the levels I intend to include in order

gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat <- factor(NA, levels=c('negative',"neutral", "positive"), ordered=TRUE)

…and then I’ll assign values to the column based on the current value of sm_effects.

gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat[gvpt_survey$sm_effects == "Extremely negative"] <- "negative"
gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat[gvpt_survey$sm_effects == "Somewhat negative"]  <- "negative"
gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat[gvpt_survey$sm_effects == "Neither positive nor negative"] <- "neutral"
gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat[gvpt_survey$sm_effects == "Somewhat positive"]  <- "positive"
gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat[gvpt_survey$sm_effects == "Extremely positive"] <- "positive"

In plain English, that first line of assigning values means “if sm_effects is”Extremely negative” then gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat should just be “negative””


We can also use the factor function to perform this re-mapping. This approach is more concise, but you have to pay very close attention to the ordering of your original factor variable.
To make this work, I’m going to create a vector called new_labels that lists, in order, the new label that we want to assign to each old value of sm_effects. Once I’ve got this, I’ll run factor again, and include labels = new_labels to assign the new value labels to my new factor variable.

new_labels <- c("negative", "negative", "neutral", "positive", "positive")

gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat <- factor(x=gvpt_survey$sm_effects, 
                          labels = new_labels,
                          ordered =TRUE
                            
                            )



Finally, if you’re comfortable with installing and loading R packages, the forcats package has a nice alternative method for doing this kind of recoding that can be more intuitive. The function is called fct_recode and the syntax will just be fct_recode(old_variable, "new label" = "old label" ...). Here’s an example:

# remember to uncomment and then run the line below to install the package:
# install.packages('forcats')

# then you'll need to run library(forcats) each time you re-open Rstudio 
# in order to load the package:

library(forcats)

gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat <-fct_recode(
  gvpt_survey$sm_effects,
  "negative" = "Extremely negative",
  "negative" = "Somewhat negative",
  "neutral" = "Neither positive nor negative"  ,
  "positive" = "Somewhat positive" ,
  "positive" = "Extremely positive" 
)




Regardless of what method you use, you’ll want to check your results after you do your recoding and make sure they align with your expectations:

# the original variable:
table(gvpt_survey$sm_effects)


           Extremely negative             Somewhat negative 
                          228                           440 
Neither positive nor negative             Somewhat positive 
                          145                           139 
           Extremely positive 
                           18 

# the recoded 3 category measure:
table(gvpt_survey$sm_effects_3cat)


negative  neutral positive 
     668      145      157

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Splitting a numeric variable
We might also want to recode numeric variables into a smaller number of categories. We can do this using the transformC function from the RCPA3 package. For instance, the variables beginning with ft_ are all feeling thermometer variables that ask respondents to rate their feelings towards a series of groups or individuals.
We can use the cut option of transformC to cut a variable into a smaller number of groups.

gvpt_survey$bad_bunny_5cat<-transformC(type='cut',               # use this option to cut a number into groups
                                  data=gvpt_survey,             # the data set 
                                  x=ft_badbunny,                # the variable we're cutting
                                  cut = c(20,40,60,80),   # the cutoff points
                                  confirm=F)              # this turns off a prompt that asks us to confirm before executing the command

# checking out the values 
table(gvpt_survey$bad_bunny_5cat)


[  0, 20) [ 20, 40) [ 40, 60) [ 60, 80) [ 80,100] 
       46        25       191       247       418 


Now we might also want to add some descriptive labels to this variable in order to make it a little more coherent in a plot or table. To do this we modify the levels attribute with a vector of labels that we want to assign to each level of the variable:

levels(gvpt_survey$bad_bunny_5cat) <- c("Very cold", "Cold", "Neutral", "Warm", "Very Warm")


table(gvpt_survey$bad_bunny_5cat)


Very cold      Cold   Neutral      Warm Very Warm 
       46        25       191       247       418

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Making a dummy
In some cases we’ll want to “dummy code” some variables to make them dichotomous.
One way to do this is using transformC with the type='dummy' option. Here’s an example of recoding the survey question about gender ID so that women are coded as a “1” and everyone else (including “prefer not to say” or “other”) are coded as “0”.

gvpt_survey$female_dummy <- transformC(type = 'dummy',
                                 x = gvpt_survey$sex_gender,
                                 response = 'Female',
                                 confirm = FALSE)

# check the results:
table(gvpt_survey$female_dummy)


  0   1 
490 523 


Another way to do this is by writing a logical expression and then converting it to a numeric variable. Converting a logical expression to numeric will automatically change all FALSE values to zero and all TRUE values to one:

# just an illustration! This isn't code you need to use anywhere

boolean_vect <- c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

as.numeric(boolean_vect)

[1] 0 0 0 1 1 1 1


These two approaches are equivalent except for some additional options offered by transformC.

gvpt_survey$female_dummy = as.numeric(gvpt_survey$sex_gender =="Female")

And don’t forget that taking the mean of a dummy will return the proportion of “1”s in that dummy variable. So we can get the % of women respondents like this:

mean(gvpt_survey$female_dummy, na.rm=T)

[1] 0.5162883


I could also create dummy variables for a more complex range of conditions. For instance, here’s how I could create a dummy variable that was equal to 1 for women who voted in 2024 and 0 for everyone else:

gvpt_survey$female_voted_dummy <- as.numeric(gvpt_survey$voted24  == "Yes" & gvpt_survey$sex_gender =="Female")

table(gvpt_survey$female_voted_dummy)


  0   1 
781 222

title: Survey import and analyses
text:
Combining Variables
In some cases it makes sense to combine one or more questions on a related topic in order to get an aggregate measure of attitudes or identify some complex combination of responses. Here are two examples of creating a new variable by combining responses from two or more survey items.

Example 1: Condition based on multiple variables
What if I wanted to do something like create an indicator variable for people who answered the survey using a Windows device and who also use social media every day to get news about politics? I could do this by using a logical statement similar to the one I used in the section on combining variables. However, in this case, I’ll write out multiple conditions and chain them together using an & operator.

gvpt_survey$sm_windows <- NA

gvpt_survey$sm_windows[gvpt_survey$sm_news == "Daily" & gvpt_survey$metadata_Operating_System == "Windows" ] <- "Daily SM user + Windows OS"
gvpt_survey$sm_windows[gvpt_survey$sm_news != "Daily" & gvpt_survey$metadata_Operating_System != "Windows" ] <- "Less than daily SM user + Non-Windows OS"
gvpt_survey$sm_windows[gvpt_survey$sm_news != "Daily" & gvpt_survey$metadata_Operating_System == "Windows" ] <- "Less than daily SM user + Windows OS"
gvpt_survey$sm_windows[gvpt_survey$sm_news == "Daily" & gvpt_survey$metadata_Operating_System != "Windows" ] <- "Daily SM user + Non-Windows OS"

table(gvpt_survey$sm_windows)


          Daily SM user + Non-Windows OS 
                                     338 
              Daily SM user + Windows OS 
                                      56 
Less than daily SM user + Non-Windows OS 
                                     506 
    Less than daily SM user + Windows OS 
                                      76 




Example 2: Additive index
There’s a series of variables labelled “trust_” that ask about a respondent’s level of trust in various institutions. We could combine all of these questions into an additive index of “general” social trust.
There’s a number of ways we could approach this problem, but for this example, I’ll just convert this ordered factor variable into a number using as.numeric. Since the factor levels are already ordered from least trusting to most trusting, I can add all of these together to get a simple additive index of the level of trust expressed by each respondent:

total_trust <-  
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_fam)  +
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_fed)  +
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_localgov)  +
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_media) +
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_police) +
  as.numeric(gvpt_survey$trust_relig)


summary(total_trust)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   8.00   14.00   16.00   16.46   19.00   30.00     136 


Note that this only works if the factors are already ordered from lowest to highest. If the levels of the factor variable follow a different ordering (or if there is a “don’t know” option) then I’ll need to be sure I correctly order the categories before I turn this into a numeric variable.


Example 3: Averaging
What if we want average over a set of numeric responses? For instance, we have a series of feeling thermometer questions that ask about Trump administration officials. We might take an average of these three questions to get a rough measure of someone’s overall support for the Trump administration. The code below selects the three feeling thermometer columns and then uses rowMeans to calculate the average for each row of the data:

admin_cols<-c("ft_trump", "ft_noem", "ft_vance")

# a vector of column names we want to extract: 

# creating a new data frame from gvpt_survey that only contains the five columns listed above:
admin_fts<-gvpt_survey[,admin_cols]

# rowMeans will calculate an average across each row of the data
avg_admin_ft<-rowMeans(admin_fts, na.rm=T)

# putting the result in its own column
gvpt_survey$avg_trumpadmin_ft <- avg_admin_ft

Now we can take a look at the distribution of the overall thermometer score:

hist(gvpt_survey$avg_trumpadmin_ft, main='Average Trump officials rating (0 - 100 scale)', xlab ='Avg')








Now we can take a look at the relationship between party ID and average thermometer ratings for these three administration officials :

compmeansC(dv= avg_trumpadmin_ft,  iv=pid_summary, data=gvpt_survey,
           xlab = 'Party ID', 
           ylab = 'Average thermometer',
           main = 'Average Trump admin. official rating (0 - 100 scale)',
           plot=FALSE
           )

title: Links
text:
Some helpful links for students interested in learning more about political science, research methods, or R programming.

Textbook Resources

PoliSciData.com

This is the website for the course textbook. In addition to helpful guides and videos, they’ve got an excellent collection of political science data sets that are free and online. If you’re interested in doing your own analyses, this is a great place to start. You might also want to check out their YouTube page.




News and Analysis

Good Authority

Good Authority is the successor to The Monkey Cage, a blog previously hosted by the Washington Post. Its a great place to read new research and analysis of current events from a polisci perspective.

LSE Blogs

Commentary and analysis of global and European politics hosted by the London School of Economics.

FiveThirtyEight

Data-driven analysis and commentary on current events and sports. Now hosted by ABC News.

Pew Research

A non-partisan think tank that tracks public opinion in the U.S. and abroad. Their Decoded Blog offers some really nice hands-on tutorials for anyone interested in working with public opinion data.




R
There are a ton of great free resources for learning more about R, and this is by no means an exhaustive list, but these are some books and tutorials that I think are especially useful if you’re interested in learning more about using R for analysis.

R for data science

This is a free e-book written, appropriately, for people who want to use R for data science. The book assumes some basic knowledge of R programming, but its an excellent resource if you want to learn how to do things like build your own database from scratch or scrape the web.

https://rforpoliticalscience.com/

A blog with short posts detailing packages, data sources, and other small projects and tips all aimed at R-using political scientists.

Big Book of R

Links to hundreds of free, open-source R tutorials arranged by topic.

title: Codebook
text:
Use the codebook below to get additional information about variables in the survey data.

Note and suggestions

Variables names beginning with meta_ contain metadata about respondents. These are things like their web browser, the amount of time they spent on the survey, and their unique response ID.
pid_summary is a 7-category measure of party ID that was created using the method we discussed in week 1: people are first asked for their party ID. Those who say they prefer Democrats or Republicans are asked about the strength of their party identification, and self-described independents are asked whether they “lean” toward one party or another, which gives us an ordinal measure of party ranging from Strong Democrat to Strong Republican.
race_ethnicity_summary is re-coded from the original race and ethnicity questions and made to resemble the race/ethnicity question on the ANES. The survey allowed respondents to check multiple boxes for their racial identity, which is why there are a series of dummy variables (race_1, race_2…), for each racial category. The survey also asked about Hispanic ethnicity in a separate question. So race_ethnicity_summary combines these responses into a single categorical variable with separate categories for multiracial and Hispanic respondents.
Variables that end with OTHER_TEXT store the answers to questions where respondents picked an “Other” option. For instance: if someone said they preferred “someone else” in the 2024 election, their write-in preference is in the variable votechoice24_OTHER_TEXT. In most cases, these responses aren’t going to be useful for your analyses because only a handful of people gave any answer.
Note that many of these questions allow respondents to give a response of not sure. You’ll want to make a decision about how you plan to handle these. One option might be to drop them entirely. Another option might be to combine the not sure responses with another response category. How you choose to handle this is up to you, but just keep in mind that you need to make some kind of decision here because keeping them as is will make ordinal variables no longer ordinal.

title: Final Survey Information
text:
Introduction
The Final Survey Write Up is an opportunity for you to showcase the skills you have developed in GVPT201. In your paper, you will take on the role of a Political Analyst, and present analyses to a politician of your choice. You will choose items from the survey we developed and create and test two hypotheses about what factors explain some outcome of interest.
Your paper will be a maximum of four pages long, single spaced. Don’t worry, we will provide plenty of resources for you to be successful. This document walks you through the process of writing your paper. As always, if you have any questions, please feel free to contact your designated teaching assistant. Also, make sure to have some fun with this assignment! It’s not every day you get to pretend to be a political consultant!

title: Final Survey Information
text:
Step 1: Choose a Topic
The first steps in writing your paper are:

choosing a politician to contact.
a name for your political consulting firm, and
the two dependent variables you wish to study and the three independent variables that you expect will explain each outcome.

Your dependent variables for the regression models should either be numeric or they should be ordinal variables with at least 5 categories (if you need to recode some values to make your variables fit this criteria, this is also fine)
Your independent variables can be ordinal, numeric, or nominal provided you understand how these will change your interpretation of the regression model. You should pick variables that you expect are likely to explain the outcome of interest or that are important to consider in accounting for spurious correlations.

title: Final Survey Information
text:
Step 2: Create an R script
Once you have identified your topic and variables, you may now begin writing an r-script.
First, you’ll want to import the final survey data and load the RCPA3 package, which you can do by running this code:

library(RCPA3)

survey <-readRDS(url('https://github.com/Neilblund/GVPT-201-Site/raw/refs/heads/main/Rdata/survey_fmted.rds'))

Next, you’ll need to do any required re-coding to make your variables useful or to simplify your analyses. For example, you might need to:

Recode “Not sure” responses as NA values and then make an ordered categorical variable numeric (Ex: dropping the “not sure” response to the left_right_scale question and then converting it to a number using as.numeric)
You may choose to transform an interval level variable to a dummy variable (Ex: 0 to 50 indicates that you do not support Trump, and 51 to 100 indicates someone does support Trump)
You might combine one or more related survey items to create an additive index. (Ex: average all of the trump_actions questions together to make an index of overall support for Trump’s policies)
Or you might collapse or drop categories of a nominal variable to simplify your analyses (Ex: creating a single dummy variable to compare respondents who identified as female vs. respondents who identified as any other option in the “sex/gender” question.

Second, for each variable, calculate basic descriptive statistics. You can do this by using both freqC and describeC. Third, create a histogram for each dependent variable. These histograms should be neatly formatted and easy to understand.
Finally, run the two regression analyses. Use the regC function for the linear regression (or logregC for logistic regression). Make sure to assign your models to an object in R and use the printC=TRUE option to store your output in a nicely formatted table that can be included in your paper.

# WRONG ! I want to store my output so I can look at it later!
regC(y ~ x, printC=TRUE)

# RIGHT! Now if I run "model1" on its own line I'll print the results from model1
model1 <- regC(y ~ x, printC=TRUE)

title: Final Survey Information
text:
Step 3: Write your paper
Once you have written your code, you can write your paper. Your paper should include the following:

Part I: Introduction/Background

A name/slogan (included in the header)
An introduction paragraph that introduces the analysis (the variables of interest, the types of analysis, the source of the data)
Explain DV1 and why it is important to the study
Explain DV2 and why it is important to the study
Two correctly labeled and professional looking histograms (to be created in R, see step 2)
Basic descriptive statistics for DV1
Basic descriptive statistics for DV2



Part II: Model 1

Discuss how IVs are coded for linear regression model 1
Provide basic descriptive statistics for IVs for linear regression model 1
Linear Regression Model output
Explain the what the results mean, including interpreting the coefficients, the p-values, and the model fit (Adjusted R-squared)



Part III: Model 2

Discuss how IVs are coded for linear regression model 2

Part IV: Conclusions

Provide at least three recommendations based on your results

Step 4: Review
After writing your paper, review to make sure you have met all the requirements listed above. Make sure your paper is free of grammatical errors and is easily readable. Then, it is highly recommended that you ask someone to review your paper. This can be your teaching assistant or a classmate.

Acknowledge any limitations or important “next steps” you might want to consider for your analysis.

Once you are confident that you have met all requirements in your paper. Your submission is due during the final exam period for your section. text:
Use the codebook below to get additional information about variables in the survey data.

Note and suggestions

Variables names beginning with meta_ contain metadata about respondents. These are things like their web browser, the amount of time they spent on the survey, and their unique response ID.
pid_summary is a 7-category measure of party ID that was created using the method we discussed in week 1: people are first asked for their party ID. Those who say they prefer Democrats or Republicans are asked about the strength of their party identification, and self-described independents are asked whether they “lean” toward one party or another, which gives us an ordinal measure of party ranging from Strong Democrat to Strong Republican.
race_ethnicity_summary is re-coded from the original race and ethnicity questions and made to resemble the race/ethnicity question on the ANES. The survey allowed respondents to check multiple boxes for their racial identity, which is why there are a series of dummy variables (race_1, race_2…), for each racial category. The survey also asked about Hispanic ethnicity in a separate question. So race_ethnicity_summary combines these responses into a single categorical variable with separate categories for multiracial and Hispanic respondents.
Variables that end with OTHER_TEXT store the answers to questions where respondents picked an “Other” option. For instance: if someone said they preferred “someone else” in the 2024 election, their write-in preference is in the variable votechoice24_OTHER_TEXT. In most cases, these responses aren’t going to be useful for your analyses because only a handful of people gave any answer.
Note that many of these questions allow respondents to give a response of not sure. You’ll want to make a decision about how you plan to handle these. One option might be to drop them entirely. Another option might be to combine the not sure responses with another response category. How you choose to handle this is up to you, but just keep in mind that you need to make some kind of decision here because keeping them as is will make ordinal variables no longer ordinal.

Regression and correlation are very close cousins. But they perform slightly different roles.


Regression lets us use a slope and intercept to summarize how X and Y are related.
Correlation uses a single number to summarize the relationship between two interval variables.
Correlation is also standardized, so that it ranges from -1 to +1, regardless of the scale of the original variables.

P < .05 means “1 in 20 results will be a Type I error”
So, what happens if I just test everything?

title: Chapter 7: Hypothesis Testing Pt II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”
Here’s a function that produces random results, runs a t-test, and then determines whether the results are significant at the .05 level:

set.seed(100)

simulate_experiment<-function(){
  N <- 100
  treatment_assignment<-rep(c("control group", "test group"), each = N/2)
  outcome<-rnorm(length(treatment_assignment))
  p<-t.test(outcome ~ treatment_assignment)$p.value
  significance <- ifelse(p < .05, "significant", "not significant")
  return(significance)
}

title: Chapter 7: Hypothesis Testing Pt II

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

The ANES has thousands of variables, so there are bound to be hundreds of combinations that will give us significant results purely by chance.
P-hacking, or trying out a bunch of models until one just gets over the threshold for significance, is bound to produce false positives.

title: Chapter 7: Hypothesis Testing Pt II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”




In published research, there are few incentives to publish a non-significant result, so people sometimes run lots of tests and only publish the ones that “work”
Which results in lots of findings that later can’t be replicated: they were just random false positives.

Exploring your data is fine (especially when you’re learning) but running more tests means you should be more skeptical of your results.
Remember that there’s nothing magical about p<.05. Interpret your p-values and confidence intervals in terms of what they mean about uncertainty, not just in terms of significance/insignificance.

text:
Review of some concepts

Mean (\(\mu\))

The (arithmetic) mean or average of a variable is the sum of every element divided by the number of observations




Standard deviation (\(\sigma\))

The standard deviation of a measure of dispersion. It tells us how much things vary around the mean.

title: Inference
text:
Review of some concepts

Standardization:

We can “mean-center” a variable by subtracting its mean from each observation. Then we can divide each observation by the standard deviation. This will give us a variable with a mean of zero and standard deviation of 1. (We’ll often refer to this standardized variable as “Z” or a “Z-score”.)


\[
\text{Z score} = \frac{\text{Deviation from the mean}}{\text{Standard Deviation}}
\]

title: Inference
text:
Distributions

Probability distribution

A probability distribution is a function that describes the probability of different random values of a variable or statistic. If I know the distribution and its parameters for something, then I can make predictions about the probability of some outcome using the probability density function for that distribution.

title: Inference
text:
The normal distribution




The normal distribution is a probability distribution that produces data that looks like this:




The normal distribution has two parameters: the mean (\(\mu\)) and standard deviation (\(\sigma\)). If we know these parameters we can calculate the area under any set of points in this curve.




So, we can use this to make predictions like “what % of observations would be 2 or Z-scores above the mean?”

title: Inference
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
When I take a decent-sized random sample a continuous variable from a population with a fixed mean:


I know the sample mean (\(\bar{x}\)) is drawn from a normal distribution.
I know the mean (\(\mu\)) of this sampling distribution is equal to the population mean.
I know the standard error of this sampling distribution is equal to \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

So: I know that 95% of my sample averages or proportions will be within \(\approx 1.96\) standard errors of the correct answer (and any number of other probabilities based on the normal curve)

title: Inference
text:
Confidence Intervals
Confidence intervals answer the question “what’s a range of values that is likely to contain the population parameter?”

title: Inference
text:
Estimating \(\sigma\)
How do we estimate a standard error for a variable when the population standard deviation is unknown?

If the sample is large enough we can use the sample standard deviation itself to estimate the population standard deviation after a tiny correction:


Population standard deviation:
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i} (x_{i} - \mu)^2}{n}}
\]


Sample standard deviation:
\[
s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i} (x_{i} - \mu)^2}{n-1}}
\]

title: Inference
text:
Estimating \(\sigma\)
We’re trying to estimate the population standard deviation using the sample standard deviation. In large samples, these are going to be very close most of the time. In very small samples, the \(s\) will be biased toward zero. So in very small samples, we would tend to underestimate uncertainty.

title: Inference
text:
Student’s T Distribution




Remember that the normal distribution has just two parameters: mean and standard deviation.




“Student’s T” distribution has an extra parameter - degrees of freedom - which is equal to the sample size minus the number of parameters we’re trying to estimate.

(For right now, this just means \(n-1\) because we’re just using the sample to estimate the population mean.)





When df is low (less than 30) the T distribution has “fatter tails”




Around df >= 30 it is basically indistinguishable from the normal.

Sampling strategies

Contemporary polls often get stuff wrong, but many general election pollsters are able to get a lot closer with far fewer observations (even as conditions get worse!) How?

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Simple Random Samples


Simple Random Samples: get a list of the entire target population, and start selecting at random.




In the old days, you might use a book like this to generate random numbers. Now we can just do it with a computer.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Simple Random Samples


Pros

We’ll converge toward representativeness +/- some random error. As we approach sample sizes of 1,000 or more, the probability of a very large random error becomes negligible.


Cons:

Where am I supposed to get a list of the entire population!?
Can be inefficient: we need a lot of data to get the margin of error to an acceptable level
What if I want to study public opinion among a small group? (felons, LGBTQ people, millionaires)

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Clustered samples



Cluster Sampling: Instead of targeting individuals, I might sample areas like a city block, census tract, or household.
Pros: Usually much easier to get a list of households rather than a list of people.
Cons: clustering typically increases sampling variability because observations within a cluster aren’t totally independent.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Stratification

Stratified Sampling divides the population into groups and then randomly sample within those groups.

For instance: I might group people by generation (Z, millennial, gen-X, etc.) and then randomly sample until I hit a target quota for generation.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Stratification



Pros: Ensuring representativeness isn’t left entirely to chance. I can even oversample certain rare groups to ensure they’re accounted for in the data.
Cons: this isn’t pure random sampling, so we’ll typically need to re-weight data to account for overrepresentation of certain groups.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Sampling strategies: Stratification and clustering

Today, most studies will use a complex combination of stratification and clustering
They’ll also use additional calibration or post-stratification methods to adjust for things like differential non-response.
This is why you need to use weights when working with NES data: they correct for these problems.

title: Samples and surveys
text: Sampling strategies: sample weighting

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Post-stratification/Calibration

The basic idea of calibration weighting is simple: if you have twice as many white college educated respondents as you would expect for a representative sample, then you just make each white college educated response count as 1/2 an observation. We call this inverse probability weighting.
The census gives us reliable targets for basic demographics like race, gender, and age.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Weighting

In practice, this can be complicated because we generally want to weight for lots of characteristics at once, or make adjustments for things (like voting history) that aren’t measured on the Census.
Differences of opinion in how/what to weight accounts for a lot of the systematic differences across public opinion surveys that ask the same questions.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Weighting

Something to keep in mind: weighting can go very wrong! Differences of opinion in how to weight things accounts for a lot of the systematic differences across public opinion surveys that ask the same questions.
Weighting can’t solve everything. Its much easier to account for things like small demographic differences compared to more complex problems like differential non-response.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Snowball Sample

Snowball Sampling is a method of surveying very small or hard-to-reach populations. Like surveys of the homeless, or drug users, or experts on medieval history. It works like a chain letter:

Survey some number of known members
Ask those members to give you the contact information for other members
Repeat N times.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Snowball Sample
There are no guarantees that a Snowball Sample won’t have the Literary Digest problem, its only viable as a research strategy because some groups are so hard to reach that they just can’t be studied any other way.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Convenience Samples

Convenience Samples are non-representative samples that simply target a population that is easy to access. (College students are a classic example)
Convenience Samples are not representative and don’t really aim to be. Instead, they’re often to used to do things like quickly test out a survey or experiment. Its unlikely they can be generalized to the population.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Convenience Samples

Online opt-in surveys have been used to estimate public opinion with some extensive re-weighting, but the results are mixed, and they definitely can produce biased results for some groups
Our class survey will be something like a mixture of snowball and convenience sampling, so we’re won’t have representative data. We’ll ignore this problem, but its definitely something to keep in mind when assessing real-world polls!

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Non-survey data
Data on countries or U.S. states seemingly aren’t really samples at all. So we don’t typically have to worry as much about issues of bias, but random error and bias will still come up.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Non-survey data

Some sources of bias for cross-national data:

Countries may not keep complete records.
Some sources may disagree on whether some countries exist.
Some national statistics may be based on surveys that have their own biases.

For our purposes, we’ll treat data sets like the “states” and “world” data sets included with your workbook as representative samples from … a potentially infinite population of states or countries.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Notes on polls

Differential non-response is still a problem, and it can vary from election to election. But its less of an issue for issue-polling (the stuff in the NES) compared to election polling.
Size doesn’t necessarily mean more accurate results. Pay attention to things like transparency of methods.

title: Samples and surveys
text:
Notes on polls

Estimating a proportion is easier than predicting an outcome. In a closely contested election, a very small miss can completely change people’s expectations about the results.
The margin of error is probably larger than what is reported because the margin only accounts for random sampling error, not bias.

Assessing Theories



Theories require simplified representations of a complex reality
Utility, not “truth”: theoretical models invariably contain assumptions and they’re probably violated in practice.





George Box: “All models are wrong, but some are useful”

title: Explanations and comparisons
text:
Theoretical Scope
Theories vary in their scope:


Early sociologists like Marx, Durkheim, Weber attempted to develop all-encompassing “laws” of political/social/historical change. These are sometimes called “grand theories”
Contemporary social sciences are less ambitious, and so its more common to propose “middle-range” theories that seek to explain a smaller number regularities in one area.

However, they may draw on “grand theories” either implicitly or explicitly.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Concepts and variables

Definition: identifying concrete features of the objects or events we’re studying and the tools to measure them.
Measurement representing real-life objects and events as variables
Description making generalizations about variables

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Variables

The results of the measurement process.
By definition a variable must vary
How we describe a variable will depend on how we measure it.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Nominal Variables


Nominal variables are categorical variables with no intrinsic ordering.
Examples include the names of countries or people, someone’s religion or racial/ethnic self id
Some nominal variables are represented by numbers, but the values of those numbers are arbitrary: zip codes, jersey numbers, and telephone numbers are still nominal because there’s no ordering to them.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Nominal Variables
The region of a particular U.S. state is a nominal variable: there’s a fixed number of categories and no intrinsic ordering

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Ordinal Variables



Ordinal variables have a small number of categories that can be ordered.
However, the gaps between differing ranks may be unequal.


Top finishing times for Boston Marathon in 2024. The placements are ordinal: the distance in time between first and second place doesn’t necessarily equal the distance between second and third.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Ordinal Variables
A common source of ordinal variables will be survey items that ask people to rate their position on a scale from “strongly agree” to “strongly disagree” or “very important” to “not at all important”.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Ordinal Variables
Another source of ordinal variables might be data that we’ve grouped into ordered categories based on another variable.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description
text:
Ordinal Variables


For instance: the World Bank classifies countries into four ordinal categories based on their per-capita GDP. There’s a clear ordering, but the spaces are not equal.

title: Chapter 2: Measurement and Description

Ordinal Variables
Two things to keep in mind when working with ordinal variables:





The “ordering” might be partly a function of your research question. You could flip these or combine categories to arrange them from “most partisan” to “least partisan”.
Some survey variables may only be ordinal after you handle people who didn’t answer the question.

text:
Interval Variables

These are just numbers. They’re measured along a continuum with equal spacing (i.e., the difference from 3 and 4 is “the same” as the difference between 6 and 7)
Examples: age, height, temperature, distance.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Terms

Conceptual Definition

A description of the concrete, measurable properties of a concept and the unit of analysis to which it applies

Unit of Analysis

The entity that that is being studied. For instance: individuals, governments, parties etc.

Operational Definition

A description of the instrument used to measure the concept

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
section: Crafting Conceptual Definitions: Unit of Analysis
text:
Crafting Conceptual Definitions: Unit of Analysis

What is the unit? What entity possesses the characteristic?

The U.S. and Canada are democracies (concept: democracy, unit: countries)
Lincoln, LBJ, and Trump are the three tallest U.S. presidents (concept: height, unit: presidents/people)
Labour is the UK’s main center-left political party (concept: party ideology/family, unit: political party)



One way to think of this: if you put your data into a spreadsheet, what does each “row” represent? The answer to that question is the unit of analysis.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
section: Unit of analysis and the ecological fallacy
text:
Unit of analysis and the ecological fallacy
The ecological fallacy occurs when you attribute a characteristic of groups to individuals. For instance:

High-income states tend to vote for Democrats, but rich people tend to vote for Republicans.
Suicide rates in 19th century Europe were higher in Protestant countries compared to Catholic countries, but Protestant individuals were no more likely to die by suicide.
In the 1930 census, zip codes with more immigrants had higher literacy rates, but immigrant individuals had lower literacy rates.

All of these are fundamentally problems of ignoring the unit of analysis.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Crafting Conceptual Definitions: Key features

What are the essential features of the concept?

If there are cases or definitions everyone agrees on, what characteristics do they share?
Are certain qualities necessary or sufficient for a case to belong to a category?
What characteristics are most distinctive to those cases?
What is most helpful for clarifying edge-cases?

Are there multiple dimensions or just one? If two characteristics always occur together, you might only need to account for one of them!

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Crafting Conceptual Definitions: transparency
We want to avoid being Potter Stewart:

The goal is cumulative knowledge, and a private definition can’t provide that.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Some steps to take:


Identify the unit of analysis
Make a list of important properties, clear examples and non-examples, and/or generally accepted definitions
Remove items that aren’t measurable
Reduce dimensions where possible (if a characteristic is shared by positive cases and negative cases, then it isn’t useful)
Refine as needed

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Measuring reliability

Split half: for a measurement using a multi-item scale, we can split results and use half the questions to predict the remaining half.

If the scale questions all measure the same “thing” then you would expect the halves to resemble each other.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Considerations: Validity

Validity refers to whether an operational definition correctly measures the concept we’re interested in.
A challenge to validity might come from cases that seem mis-categorized in our definition. For example: the minimalist definition of democracy suggests that Japan was authoritarian for much of the latter half of the 20th century.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Considerations: Validity and Reliability

Measures could be reliable but invalid: your astrological sign is a reliable measure of your political views because it doesn’t change, but it also isn’t valid because it has no real correspondence to your actual politics.
Measures could be valid but unreliable: an exam with a single well-written question might be a valid measure of a student’s understanding of material, but it will probably have more random variability compared to an exam with multiple poorly-written questions.

title: Chapter 1: Concepts and definitions
text:
Measurement Error

Measurement error is a source of noise, systematic measurement error is a source of bias
We’ll generally find that random noise is much easier to deal with than bias because we can simply collect more data. Significant bias, on the other hand, presents profound challenges to research because we can only correct it if we can measure it

“In my opinion, the outcome of Biden winning is so statistically improbable, that it is not possible to dismiss fraud and biased changes in the ways ballots were processed, validated, and tabulated” - Charles Cicchetti


The math checks out! So what’s wrong with this claim?

How not to use a p-value

if the objective is to assess whether Biden won legitimately, then it is beside the point whether Biden and Clinton enjoyed the same expected support. Support can differ across candidates for any number of reasons, and it is absurd to think that any such difference constitutes evidence of election fraud. -Eggers, Garro, and Grimmer

(the authors go on to note that they can reject this null in every state in every presidential election since 1960)

This tells us that differences across elections aren’t random, but that’s probably not the most important question for researchers!

What hypothesis testing does


In experimental research, “treatment” is randomly assigned, so once we’ve eliminated “random chance”, we can conclude the difference is due to the treatment.

title: Significance testing Part II

What hypothesis testing does



In observational research, ruling out random chance is just the first step towards identifying a cause
We’d need to rule out a lot of other more plausible explanations here first.

title: Significance testing Part II

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”
Lots of causes, but bad hypothesis testing plays a role:


P < .05 means “1 in 20 results will be a Type I error”
So, what happens if I just test everything?

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”
Here’s a function that produces random results, runs a t-test, and then determines whether the results are significant at the .05 level:

set.seed(100)

simulate_experiment<-function(){
  N <- 100
  treatment_assignment<-rep(c("control group", "test group"), each = N/2)
  outcome<-rnorm(length(treatment_assignment))
  p<-t.test(outcome ~ treatment_assignment)$p.value
  significance <- ifelse(p < .05, "significant", "not significant")
  return(significance)
}

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”
If I run this function 100 times, I’ll get about 5 significant results:


p_values<-replicate(n=100, expr = simulate_experiment())
barplot(table(p_values), main = "Significance tests for 100 simulated experiments")










but there’s definitely not a relationship here. This is random noise!

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

The ANES has thousands of variables, so there are bound to be hundreds of combinations that will give us significant results purely by chance.
P-hacking, or trying out a bunch of models until one just gets over the threshold for significance, is bound to produce false positives.

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
P-hacking and the “replication crisis”



In published research, there are few incentives to publish a non-significant result, so people sometimes run lots of tests and only publish the ones that “work”
Which results in lots of findings that later can’t be replicated: they were just random false positives.





Z-values in pubished papers in medical research from: van Zwet, Erik W., and Eric A. Cator. “The significance filter, the winner’s curse and the need to shrink.” Statistica Neerlandica 75.4 (2021): 437-452.

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
Best practices when conducting research


Exploring your data is fine (especially when you’re learning) but running more tests means you should be more skeptical of your results.
Remember that there’s nothing magical about p<.05.

title: Significance testing Part II
text:
Best practices when reading research


As a reader, you should be cautious when you see a result that just barely meets the criteria for significance, especially if its:

Not supported by additional replications or the hypothesis wasn’t pre-registered
Un-intuitive or not based on some pre-existing theory or reasonable expectation
Substantively small and/or based on a small sample

Rival Explanations

How can we distinguish correlation from causation?
This process inevitably requires us to consider rival explanations for an observed relationship:

For instance: if I find that social media use correlated with a lower likelihood of turning out to vote, I might ask whether age is a confounder that could explain this correlation.

title: Research Design

Experiments

Experiments use random assignment to account for rival explanations. If you randomly assign people to receive a “treatment”, then you can ensure that there is no confounding because nothing is correlated with your IV.

Field experiments can face fewer external validity problems, but some things still can’t be experimentally manipulated.

title: Significance testing
text:
Testing a hypothesis



Of course, its possible that there’s a real relationship here, but its also possible to produce disparities this large just by random chance.
Hypothesis testing answers the question: “can we rule out random error as a plausible explanation for our results?”

title: Significance testing
text:
Null vs. Alternative Hypothesis
There are really two “sides” of our hypothesis:


Alternative/Research hypothesis(\(H_a\)) : “X and Y are related”, “X influences Y”, or “this outcome is not random”




Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): “no relationship”, “no effect” or “no better than random chance”

title: Significance testing
text:
Null vs. Alternative Hypothesis

Technically, we don’t really test the research hypothesis \(H_a\). Instead we’ll try to rule out \(H_0\) by asking “how likely are results like these if the null is true?”



We can either fail to reject the null, meaning we can’t rule it out, or reject the null, meaning it’s unlikely to have produced data like what we’re seeing.

title: Significance testing
text:
Type I and II error
When trying to make a judgement about \(H_0\), there are two ways to be wrong:





Type I errors: X and Y are unrelated, but we reject \(H_0\). (False positive)
Type II errors: X and Y are actually related, but we fail to reject \(H_0\). (False negative)

Type I and II error


In general, we’re more concerned with Type I error, so we put a relatively high burden of evidence for showing things are related, even if that means we’ll sometimes get false negatives.

title: Significance testing
text:
What hypothesis testing won’t do


Hypothesis testing won’t tell us “there’s 0% chance that randomness produced this result”. There’s always some possibility that random error produced something.
It also doesn’t tell us whether we have a spurious correlation or a biased sample.
It won’t tell us the probability of any hypothesis. It only tells us the probability of a result if a hypothesis is true.

title: Significance testing
text:
The P-value method
P-values are one of two ways that we can determine whether to reject the null hypothesis

(we’ll talk about the other method, confidence intervals, in a later class)

title: Significance testing
section: Hypothesis testing: general steps for P-values
text:
Hypothesis testing: general steps for P-values



State \(H_0\) and \(H_a\)
Decide on threshold for significance, sometimes called \(\alpha\) (alpha).

(.1, .05, and .01 are common thresholds.)

Run the test and calculate a p-value.

\(p \gt \alpha\) means the result is not statistically significant at your threshold. You fail to reject the null.
A \(p \leq \alpha\) means the result is statistically significant. You can reject the null.

title: Significance testing
text:
An experimental hypothesis test
Can our subject distinguish tap water from bottled?


Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): the subject can reliably identify bottled water and tap water.
Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): the subject is guessing

title: Significance testing
text:
The Lady Tasting Tea


R.A Fisher lays out an experiment along these lines in a 1935 book.
(in that case, it was a psychologist who said she could tell whether a cup of tea was poured milk-first or tea-first)(Fisher et al. 1956)




Muriel Bristol-Roach

title: Significance testing
text:
Our experiment
Experimental Setup:


8 glasses of water.
4 are tap water 🚰, and 4 are bottled 💧

the subject knows how many of each, but not which is which

The subject tastes all 8 and categorizes them, then the researcher counts the number of correct vs. incorrect.

title: Significance testing
text:
Our hypothesis test
Our p-value here will be calculated based on the number of cups correctly classified as tap or bottled.

So:


P =.20 would be “a 20% chance of classifying X or more cups correctly under the null hypothesis (guessing at random)”
We’ll set an \(\alpha = .05\). So we will fail to reject the null hypothesis if there’s over a 5% chance that someone guessing at random could do as well (or better) than the subject.

title: Significance testing
text:
Fisher’s Exact Test

Fisher’s proposed test is non-parametric, it doesn’t require any assumptions about distributions or infinity or repeated sampling. Instead, we’re going to calculate an exact probability based on counting all the ways a random guess could generate different outcomes. We’ll need to calculate:


The number of ways to choose 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 cups correctly




The total number of combinations of four cups.

title: Significance testing
text:
P-value notes


Things that are true of all P-values, regardless of the test:

They represent the probability of something under the null hypothesis. This is not the same thing as the probability of the alternative hypothesis.
They don’t tell you anything about the probability of bias or spuriousness.
You can fail to reject the null because there’s no relationship, but you can also fail to reject it because you don’t have enough data.
We’ll often look for a p-value of \(\leq.05\), but there’s nothing special about 5%. This is a “conventional level of statistical significance” largely because R.A. Fisher came up with it.

title: Inference
text:
Margin of error


The margin of error is more frequently called a confidence interval in statistics.
A confidence interval is a range that we are reasonably certain contains the actual population value.

Specifically, the margin generally reported is a 95% confidence interval.
If I estimate that 50% of respondents are Democrats with a margin of error of +/- 3% then I’m saying I’m 95% certain that the range 47-53% contains the correct percentage of Democrats in the population.

title: Inference
text:
Margin of error = Confidence Interval
Technically, 95% confidence means: “if I repeated this survey an infinite number of times and recalculated the CI for each one, 95% of my calculated confidence intervals would contain the actual population value.”

title: Inference
text:
Margin of error = Confidence Interval


We generally aren’t bothering to sample anything repeatedly, so how do we know this?

The main reason we’re able to calculate a confidence interval is because we actually know a lot about how random errors “behave” in repeated sampling thanks to the central limit theorem.

title: Inference
text:
Uncertainty and sampling
The general intuition:


more data = less dispersion. Estimates from a really big representative sample are going to be more likely to approximate the true population mean.
less variance = less dispersion. If people in the target population are pretty much the same, then it is more likely that a given sample will resemble the target population.

title: Inference
text:
Sampling distributions
We don’t expect the sample stat to exactly equal a population parameter, we expect it to have some error.
\[\text{Sample error} = \text{Population Parameter} - \text{Sample statistic} \]
The error is random, even though the population parameter is fixed, so if we sample repeatedly from the same population, we’ll get slightly different results each time.

title: Inference
text:
Sampling distributions

The sampling distribution describes the distribution of sample statistics across infinite samples of size \(n\) from a given population.
In other words, if I ran the exact same survey millions of times on different random samples, and recorded the same statistic from each run, how would those results be distributed?

title: Inference
section: The Sampling distribution of coin flips
text:
The Sampling distribution of coin flips
Think about flipping a coin:


the probability of landing on heads is 50% (this is our population parameter)
We’ll run an “experiment” where we flip a coin 50 times and calculate the proportion of heads.

(remember that, for a dummy (0, 1) coded dichotomous outcome, the proportion = the mean)

title: Inference
section: The Sampling distribution of coin flips
text:
The Sampling distribution of coin flips

# simulating flipping 50 coins: 
coinflips <- sample(c("heads","tails"), size=50, replace=TRUE)
# counting the number of heads
prop_heads<-mean(coinflips=='heads')



the proportion of heads is 0.38.
The error is .5 - 0.38 = -0.12

# counting the number of heads
prop_heads <- mean(coinflips=='heads')



the proportion of heads is 0.51.
The error is .5 - 0.51 = 0.01

The sampling distribution of coin flips
Repeating this experiment 5,000 times will give us a sense of the sampling distribution for this sample statistic:

# 5000 "samples" of the coin-flipping experiment
trials<-replicate(5000, sample(c("heads","tails"), size=50, replace=TRUE)=="heads")
# get the average num of heads in each trial. Expected value = .5
mean_heads <- colMeans(trials)
# draw a histogram
hist(mean_heads, main ='proportion of heads in 50 coin flips', breaks=30)

text:
The sampling distribution of coin flips





The samples are centered around the expected proportion of .5 heads




More extreme errors are less common than small ones




The results are symmetric: there are about as many high values as low ones.




Error = Sample Mean - Population Mean, so the distribution of errors has this same shape, but its centered around zero.

Coin flips technically follow a binomial distribution, but our sampling distribution looks a lot like a normal “bell-curve” centered on .5

title: Inference
text:
Sampling distributions of sample means
The central limit theorem says repeated samples from a population with a fixed mean will always end up looking like this regardless of the actual population distribution.

title: Inference
text:
The normal distribution
We know a lot about normal distributions. If we have mean \(\mu\) and a standard deviation \(\sigma\), we can easily find how much data we expect to fall anywhere within this shape using the probability density function of the normal distribution:

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
  \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{\!2}\,\right)\]


(Maybe not the kind of thing you want to calculate in your head, but pretty easy for a computer)

title: Inference
text:
The normal distribution

      )

title: Inference
text:
The normal distribution
The mean (\(\mu\)) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) will depend on the data, but we can always:


Mean center: subtract the mean \(\mu\) from each observation so that the new mean is zero.




Standardize: divide each observation by the standard deviation of the sampling distribution (\(\sigma\)), so the new standard deviation is 1



We’ll call this new number the “Z-score”:
\[
\text{Z score} = \frac{\text{Deviation from the mean}}{\text{Standard Deviation}}
\]

text:
The Central Limit Theorem







Central Limit Theorem


As the number of repeated samples approaches infinity, the sampling distribution of the mean will converge toward a normal distribution centered on the population mean.







The sampling errors will also have a normal distribution centered on zero.
Sampling errors/means are normally distributed even if the population is non-normal.
We can calculate the proportion of data that falls under different parts of the curve, provided we know \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\)

title: Inference
text:
Using the CLT
We don’t need to take infinite samples to make use of this! We can draw a sample and assume that it comes from a distribution with this shape:

title: Inference
text:
Using the CLT
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\color{red}{\sigma}\sqrt{2\pi}}
  \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\color{red}{\mu}}{\color{red}{\sigma}}\right)^{\!2}\,\right)\]


We don’t know our population mean \(\mu\), but we do know that the mean sampling error is zero.
We still need to know the standard deviation of the sampling errors. We’ll call this value our standard error or SE for short.
(We can make some simple assumptions here to get a “worst case scenario” for a survey statistic.)

title: Inference
text:
The standard error
Remember that more observations = more certainty. So we expect that the standard error will decrease when taking larger samples.

title: Inference
text:
The standard error
We actually know how much the SE shrinks for each observation:

\[
\text{Standard error (SE)} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

text:
The standard error of a proportion

\[
\text{Standard error (SE)} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]


We don’t know \(\sigma\), but surveys are usually reporting a proportion or percentage of people giving a particular response. The standard error of a proportion actually depends on the proportion itself:

\[
\text{Standard Error of a proportion} = \frac{\sqrt{p\times(1-p)}}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{p\times(1-p)}{n}}
\]

\[
p = \text{the proportion}
\]

The standard error of a proportion


Note that this part of the formula is at its maximum when p = .5 (i.e. when there’s a 50/50 split on a yes/no question)

\[
\text{Standard Error of a proportion} = \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{p\times(1-p)}}{n}}
\]


So, if we know our sample size, we can calculate the worst case scenario for the standard error where \(p = .5\)

title: Inference
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
When I take a decent-sized random sample from the population:


I know the sample mean (\(\bar{x}\)) is drawn from a normal distribution.
I know the mean of this sampling distribution is equal to the population mean.
I know the standard deviation of this sampling distribution (a.ka. the standard error) is equal to \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

So: I know that 95% of my sample averages will be within \(\approx 1.96\) standard errors of the correct answer (and any number of other probabilities based on the normal curve)

title: Significance testing
text:
Review: Null hypothesis significance testing
In a previous class, we used an experiment to examine a hypothesis about the ability to distinguish tap water from bottled.

In that test, we had a pair of hypotheses like this:

Alternative/Research hypothesis (\(H_a\)): the subject can tell whether a cup contains bottled water or tap water.
Null hypothesis \(H_0\): the subject can’t tell, and they’re just guessing.

title: Significance testing
text:
Tests for a single proportion
In the past, polls have found that a majority of the public opposed abolishing ICE.
However, this may have changed in the last few months, particularly in the wake of two high profile shootings of U.S. citizens by ICE/CBP agents.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): Support for abolishing ICE is greater than 50% (\(\rho_{\text{support} \gt .50}\))
Null hypothesis \(H_0\): Support for abolishing ICE is less than or equal to 50% (\(\rho_{\text{support} \leq .50}\))

title: Significance testing
text:
Directional hypotheses

Note that we specified a directional hypothesis about the proportion of people who support abolishing ICE.
What if our null hypothesis is that support is greater than 50% instead of less than 50%?

title: Significance testing
text:
Two-tailed tests

What if our hypothesis doesn’t specify a direction? In other words: our null hypothesis is that support for abolishing ICE is \(50\%\), the alternative is that abolishing ICE \(\neq50\%\).
This is commonly called a “two tailed test”

title: Significance testing
text:
Confidence intervals

Confidence intervals are based on the same general intuitions, and so they can also be used as a way to express a hypothesis test.
If something is significant under the p.value method it will also be significant under an equivalent confidence interval method, and vice-versa.

title: Significance testing
section: Tests for a single proportion in R
text:
Tests for a single proportion in R

In last year’s class survey of 1,316 adults, 76% of respondents in a sample said they voted in the 2024 election.
In the 2024 election, adult turnout was estimated closer to 59%.
So what is the probability of getting an error of \(\pm17\) in a sample with 1,316 people?

title: Significance testing
text:
Two sample proportions

The previous examples looked at the chances of getting some result under an assumed null hypothesis.
More often, though, we want to test a hypothesis about the difference between two groups: Are women more likely to favor abortion rights? Are retirees more likely to support social security? Are authoritarian countries more likely to start wars? etc.
These are examples of two sample tests, where we’re trying to determine whether and observed difference between to groups is the result of random sampling error.

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
Example



What factors influence whether a mass campaign succeeds or fails?
Do goals, tactics, external support etc. really make a difference?

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
Example



NAVCO 1.2: Each row represents a mass movement or campaign where participants demanded fundamental changes to the constitutional order in their country (such as regime change or secession.)
Data on campaigns from 1946 through 2014.

text:
Example: NAVCO



There’s a clear disparity in the success rates depending on the type of goal the movement is pursuing.
But could the disparity we see here be explained by random sampling error?
A difference of of proportions test doesn’t really work here because we have a 3-category IV.

text:
Example NAVCO
\(H_a\): Goal types are related to movement success
\(H_0\): Goal types are not related to movement success

What would this table look like under the null hypothesis?

Example NAVCO



If \(H_0\) is true, we would expect a table with the same marginal (row/column) totals, but without these disparities in cell frequencies.

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
Calculating a null table
We can calculate this for each cell with the formula:
\[
\text{Row Total} \times \frac{\text{Column Total}}{\text{Total Number of observations}}
\]

title: Tests for categorical variables

Calculating a null table
Note that there’s no discrepancy here when we calculate column percentages.

section: Comparing the observed to the null table
text:
Comparing the observed to the null table
Now, we need to calculate a test statistic that reflect how much the observed table differs from the table we expect under the null hypothesis.

We can get this by calculating the following for each cell and then summing up our result:
\[
\frac{(\text{observed}-\text{expected})^2}{\text{expected}}
\]

title: Tests for categorical variables
section: Comparing the observed to the null table
text:
Comparing the observed to the null table






Summing up, we get: \(0.9 + 1.1 + 8.8 + 11.7 + 0.7 + 1 = 24.2\). This is our \(\chi^2\) statistic for this table.

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
The \(\chi^2\) statistic

Summing up, we get: \(0.9 + 1.1 + 8.8 + 11.7 + 0.7 + 1 = 24.2\). This is our \(\chi^2\) statistic for this table.


Now we just need to calculate the degrees of freedom to find the p-value associated with this \(\chi^2\) statistic.


The degrees of freedom for this test is based on the number of rows and columns in the table:
\[
\text{Degrees of freedom} = (\text{number of rows} - 1 ) \times (\text{number of columns} - 1)
\]


\[
(\text{2} - 1 ) \times (\text{3} - 1) = 2
\]

What is the probability of a \(\chi^2\) statistic \(\geq 24.2\) at \(df = 2\)?

pchisq(24.2, df = 2, lower.tail=F)
