title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
\(\chi^2\) limitations and notes

\(\chi^2\) is not a “directional” test. The null hypothesis is always “no relationship”, and the alternative is just “some relationship”.
\(\chi^2\) is a continuous distribution, but cell frequencies are counts. At larger sample sizes, this doesn’t matter, but it becomes a problem when expected cell frequencies are less than 5. At very small sample sizes, Fisher’s Exact test may be better.
We can also perform a \(\chi^2\) test with a control variable by dis-aggregating based on some other characteristic and then computing the test separately for each group, but note that this can lead to the small-cell size problem.

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
\(\chi^2\) controlled comparison

We can also perform a \(\chi^2\) test with a control variable by dis-aggregating based on some other characteristic and then computing the test separately for each group to see if the relationship still exists.
For instance, what if we thought that the use of violence tactics was a confounder that actually explained the observed disparity in success rates across movement goals?

text: Controlled comparison

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
Controlled comparison

Controlled comparisons can work here, but we quickly run into a problem of small cell counts.
For small sample sizes and a small number of categories, we can use Fisher’s exact test.
But if we think there are multiple confounders, we’ll either need very large samples or we’ll need to adopt a separate approach.

title: Tests for categorical variables
text:
PRE and other measures

Lambda is one of many measures that can tell you “how much better” you can predict one categorical variable by knowing values of categorical variable. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating stronger associations.
Somers’ D measures ordinal-ordinal associations by counting “concordant” and “discordant” pairs in a cross tab.
Cramer’s V is a scaled measure based on \(\chi^2\) that also ranges from 0 to 1 and measures the strength of assocation between two categorical variables.

title: Correlation and Regression
text:
Standard error of a slope
\(S_{yx}\) represents the “standard error of the regression”. Note that the numerator here is the same as the error sum of squares.
\[
S_{yx} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{(\hat{y_i} - y_i)^2}}{n-2}}
\]

The denominator here accounts for the amount of variation in X. Note that more variability in X means that we will have a smaller standard error.
\[
SE(\beta_1) = \frac{s_{yx}}{\sqrt{\sum^n_{i=1}{(X_i -\bar{X})^2}}}
\]

title: Correlation and Regression
text:
Standard error of the intercept
We can also calculate the standard error for the intercept, but generally speaking we don’t care because we rarely test hypotheses about the intercept.
\[
SE(\hat{\beta}_0) = s_{yx} \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{X}^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})^2}}
\]

R-squared: model fit
We often want to talk about how well a model “fits” the data. \(R^2\) is one way to evaluate this.


\(R^2\) value is the proportion of variance in Y explained by variance in our independent variables.
\(R^2\) will always range from 0 to 1. Its a proportion. A score of 1 would mean that our model perfectly predicts Y.
You can think of \(R^2\) as a measure of how well the model predicts outcomes.

section: Why am I getting Error: object __ not found?
text:
Why am I getting Error: object __ not found?
Okay, there could be lots of reasons for this error message, but the most common cause is that you’ve either:

Mis-spelled a variable name.
Referenced a variable without specifying the data set where that variable is stored.
Referenced a variable that is not yet available in R.

When you reference a variable in R, it searches for that variable in the current environment, and it returns an error message when it can’t find it. So the code below returns and error because x hasn’t been defined yet:

x

Error: object 'x' not found


To access xI first need to create it by assigning a value (in this case, some text in quotation marks) to that name. This works just fine:

x<-"I am a variable"

x

[1] "I am a variable"


The other place this comes up is when you try to access a column from a data set without specifying the data set where that variable exists. For instance, “age” is a column in the nes data, but just typing “age” doesn’t work because R doesn’t know where to look:

mean(age, na.rm=T)

Error: object 'age' not found


Using the dataset$varname syntax solves this problem:

mean(nes$age, na.rm=T)

title: FAQs
text:
What are factor variables?
A factor variable is R’s default data type for storing categorical data. Technically, a factor is actually just a bunch of integers with a special levels attribute that specifies the labels that those integers correspond to:

example_factor <- factor(c(1,1,2,2,3,4), labels = c('A', 'B', 'C', 'D'))
example_factor

[1] A A B B C D
Levels: A B C D


R can also just store regular text data, but factors have some distinct advantages when working with certain data sources. The most important is that they allow us to control the ordering of tables and graphs. For example, if I make a table with a character variable, R prints the elements in alphabetical order:

string_vector <- c("Disagree", "Neither disagree nor agree", "Agree")
table(string_vector)

string_vector
                     Agree                   Disagree 
                         1                          1 
Neither disagree nor agree 
                         1 


But alphabetizing this doesn’t make sense because the variable has a clear ordering from disagree to agree. The “levels” attribute on a factor allows me to preserve that ordering:

factor_vector <- factor(string_vector, 
                        # list of the levels the order I want them to appear: 
                        levels =c("Disagree", "Neither disagree nor agree", "Agree"))

table(factor_vector)

factor_vector
                  Disagree Neither disagree nor agree 
                         1                          1 
                     Agree 
                         1 


Since each level of a factor also has a numeric value, we can also do things like calculate the median value of an ordered variable:

median(as.numeric(factor_vector))

title: Final paper FAQs
text:
What variables should I use?
This is (almost) entirely up to you! Remember that there’s a detailed codebook on the course website that describes each variable and its values. As long as you can use a linear or logistic model for it, you can use it.
However, there are a few things you should probably consider when selecting variables:

Variable types: for a linear model, your dependent variable should be numeric or you should be able to treat it as numeric (5 or more ordered categories). Your independent variables can be numeric, ordinal or categorical.
Interest and intuition: you’re not necessarily being graded on the novelty of plausibility of your theory, but you’ll find its easier to write a paper if you can make an argument for why you think a relationship would exist between your selected variables.
Conceptual/Operational definitions: You should try to make your operational definition match your conceptual definition as closely as possible. You have some wiggle room here: you might use views on the Paris Climate accords as a rough proxy for people’s concern about climate change, but you would need to be open about the fact that this is only an indirect measure for the thing you’re theorizing about. On the other hand, you should avoid using an indirect measure if there’s a clearly better option available. For example: if your theory is all about party identification, you should probably use the variable that asks directly about party ID instead of a variable that asks about how feelings towards Trump.

title: Final paper FAQs
section: My results weren’t statistically significant! What should I do?
text:
My results weren’t statistically significant! What should I do?
You are not obligated to find statistically significant results. As long as you make a reasonable argument for why your hypothesis is worth testing, this is completely fine.
If you do find that your hypothesis isn’t supported, you still need to interpret the coefficients, plot the results etc. and then acknowledge that your results don’t support your hypothesis. In the concluding section of the paper, you would also want to talk about why you think your hypothesis wasn’t supported. A few plausible reasons are:

you’re wrong
there’s not enough data
there’s uncontrolled confounding1
sampling bias

You don’t need to give a definitive explanation, just show you’re thinking about your results and that you understand what it means to reject or not reject the null hypothesis.

title: Final paper FAQs
section: How can I make sure my code is replicable?
text:
How can I make sure my code is replicable?
Before submitting your R-code, its a good idea to double-check and make sure everything runs properly. The best way to do this is:

Restart R and clear the environment. To restart R, you can press Ctrl + Shift + F10, or just close and reopen R-Studio.
Clear the environment, just press the little broom 🧹 icon in the environment pane at the top right, or enter the following command into the console:


rm(list = ls())


Run each line of code in your script, in order, one line at a time. Watch the console to make sure no error messages pop up and that you see your expected output.

How should I format my plots and tables?
If you copy output directly from R into a word processor, you’ll end up with something that looks like this:



Avoid this! Copying output directly from the R console will usually give you very wonky text.


This is not great. Most word processors use variable width fonts. These are make prose text more readable, but they mess up the alignment in plots and tables. Instead of just copy-pasting the output, you either:

Create a table and enter the values yourself.
Use an R function to create formatted regression output.

Option 2 will probably be the easiest approach for most of you. Fortunately, you can get formatted output for most RCPA3 functions by adding the printC=TRUE optional command to a function.
For instance, instead of running:

# Running without printC

library(RCPA3)
model<-regC(carfatal ~ urban, data=states)
model

I would just add printC=TRUE as an additional argument:

# Running the model with printC = TRUE
library(RCPA3)
model<-regC(carfatal ~ urban, data=states, printC=TRUE)
model

When you do this, you’ll see some text show up in the console that looks like:
Statement appended to Table.Output.Apr1126.html in C:/Users/neilb/Documents/UMD/GVPT201/GVPT201 Spring 2026
Go into the file location listed in this output and you should see a file called something like Table.Output.Apr1126.html. Click it and you should see formatted regression output. From here, you can actually just copy the coefficients table and paste it into a Word or Google doc, and it should come through looking fine.






Alternatives to RCPA3



If you’re comfortable working with R packages and syntax, there are lots of alternatives you could use to create formatted regression output. I personally like modelsummary.

title: Final paper FAQs
section: What is the most important stuff to tell readers?
text:
What is the most important stuff to tell readers?
Resist the temptation to write your analysis as a minute-by-minute account of everything you did to put the paper together. You should tell readers the things they need to know to understand your analysis; you don’t need to tell them everything you did to conduct your analysis.
For instance, here’s an example of extraneous detail:


Extraneous Detail


My variable was initially called paris_climate, but I recoded it to a numeric variable and called it paris_climate_numeric




It’s important to tell readers when your treating ordinal variables as numeric, but they typically don’t need to know what a variable used to be called in R to interpret any part of your analysis. Instead, you can just say something like “We asked respondents about whether they agreed or disagreed with the U.S. re-joining the Paris climate accords. Possible responses ranged from Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree. For the analysis, these values were recoded to a 7-point numeric scale, with 1 indicating ‘strong disagreement’ and 7 indicating ‘strong agreement’”

But it’s entirely possible that there’s some other confounding variable that wasn’t included in the data, in which case it’s fine to say “I suspect this matters, but I can’t test it with the available data”↩︎

Note and suggestions

Variables names beginning with meta_ contain metadata about respondents. These are things like their web browser, the amount of time they spent on the survey, and their unique response ID.
pid_summary is a 7-category measure of party ID that was created using the method we discussed in week 1: people are first asked for their party ID. Those who say they prefer Democrats or Republicans are asked about the strength of their party identification, and self-described independents are asked whether they “lean” toward one party or another, which gives us an ordinal measure of party ranging from Strong Democrat to Strong Republican.
race_ethnicity_summary is re-coded from the original race and ethnicity questions and made to resemble the race/ethnicity question on the ANES. The survey allowed respondents to check multiple boxes for their racial identity, which is why there are a series of dummy variables (race_1, race_2…), for each racial category. The survey also asked about Hispanic ethnicity in a separate question. So race_ethnicity_summary combines these responses into a single categorical variable with separate categories for multiracial and Hispanic respondents.
Variables that end with OTHER_TEXT store the answers to questions where respondents picked an “Other” option. For instance: if someone said they preferred “someone else” in the 2024 election, their write-in preference is in the variable votechoice24_OTHER_TEXT. In most cases, these responses aren’t going to be useful for your analyses because only a handful of people gave any answer.
Note that many of these questions allow respondents to give a response of not sure. You’ll want to make a decision about how you plan to handle these. One option might be to drop them entirely. Another option might be to combine the not sure responses with another response category. How you choose to handle this is up to you, but just keep in mind that you need to make some kind of decision here because keeping them as is will make ordinal variables no longer ordinal.

title: Codebook
text:
Use the codebook below to get additional information about variables in the survey data.

Note and suggestions

Variables names beginning with meta_ contain metadata about respondents. These are things like their web browser, the amount of time they spent on the survey, and their unique response ID.
pid_summary is a 7-category measure of party ID that was created using the method we discussed in week 1: people are first asked for their party ID. Those who say they prefer Democrats or Republicans are asked about the strength of their party identification, and self-described independents are asked whether they “lean” toward one party or another, which gives us an ordinal measure of party ranging from Strong Democrat to Strong Republican.
race_ethnicity_summary is re-coded from the original race and ethnicity questions and made to resemble the race/ethnicity question on the ANES. The survey allowed respondents to check multiple boxes for their racial identity, which is why there are a series of dummy variables (race_1, race_2…), for each racial category. The survey also asked about Hispanic ethnicity in a separate question. So race_ethnicity_summary combines these responses into a single categorical variable with separate categories for multiracial and Hispanic respondents.
Variables that end with OTHER_TEXT store the answers to questions where respondents picked an “Other” option. For instance: if someone said they preferred “someone else” in the 2024 election, their write-in preference is in the variable votechoice24_OTHER_TEXT. In most cases, these responses aren’t going to be useful for your analyses because only a handful of people gave any answer.
Note that many of these questions allow respondents to give a response of not sure. You’ll want to make a decision about how you plan to handle these. One option might be to drop them entirely. Another option might be to combine the not sure responses with another response category. How you choose to handle this is up to you, but just keep in mind that you need to make some kind of decision here because keeping them as is will make ordinal variables no longer ordinal.

You’ll typically use a weighting variable when you’re working with survey data. In this course, the nes data set will include a weight variable (wt), but there aren’t any weights for the world or states data sets.
Weighting is used to make samples more closely resemble a target population. For instance, the NES has slightly more women respondents than you would expect from a true random sample from the general population so including the weighting variable makes the responses from men count more and the responses from women count slightly less.

This concern isn’t really relevant for the world and states data sets because these aren’t samples: the states data set has data on the entire population of U.S. states, and the world data set has data on (more or less) all the countries.



They svyglm function is used to run a weighted regression, but the final project data doesn’t have any weights associated with it, so you don’t need any of the svy commands to do your analysis. Keep in mind, however, that these data are still not representative of the general population, so you should acknowledge that this is a non-random sample when you discuss your results.



You are not obligated to find statistically significant results. As long as you make a reasonable argument for why your hypothesis is worth testing, this is completely fine. If you do find that your hypothesis isn’t supported, you still need to interpret the coefficients, plot the results etc. you just need to say that you’ve failed to reject the null. In the concluding section of the paper, you would also want to talk about why you think your hypothesis wasn’t supported. A few plausible reasons are: you’re wrong, there’s not enough data, there’s uncontrolled confounding, or the sample is biased. You don’t need to give a definitive explanation, just show you’re thinking about your results and that you understand what it means to reject or not reject the null hypothesis.
(If you think there’s uncontrolled confounding and it comes from a variable that already exists in the data, you might as well test it! But its entirely possible that there’s some other confounding variable that wasn’t included in the data, in which case its fine to say “I suspect this matters, but I can’t test it”)



Before submitting your R-code, its a good idea to double-check and make sure everything runs properly. The best way to do this is: restart R, press little broom icon in the environment pane to make sure you’ve cleared all of the your data out, and then run your script one line at a time and make sure that you don’t see any errors. text:
Cook’s Distance
How big is the problem?
One way to quantify an outlier is to calculate the effect of dropping an observation on the results. Cooks D for observation i is:
\[D_i = \frac{\sum^n_{j=1}(\hat{Y_j} - \hat{Y_{j(i)}})^2}{MSE}\]

\(\hat{Y_j}\) the prediction for observation j from the full regression
\(\hat{Y_{j(i)}}\) the prediction for observation j after eliminating observation i
\(MSE\) the mean squared error of the regression

So, higher values mean that observation i is exerting more influence on our results.

A rule of thumb suggests examining outliers that have a D value over \(4/n\) where \(n\) is the number of observations
